extracted.intended_audience: chemical manufacturers, importers, distributors, employers, small business stakeholders, and regulatory analysts concerned with OSHA Hazard Communication Standard (HCS) compliance
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and analytic criteria used in OSHA's Final Economic Analysis (FEA) for revisions to the Hazard Communication Standard, including cost/savings estimation, sensitivity testing, regulatory alternatives, small-entity screening, and FRFA/FRFSA requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Released-for-shipment cost savings estimation
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate the percentage loss avoided due to the released-for-shipment provision as the product of four factors: (1) the costs of relabeling as a percentage of the value of the products requiring relabeling; (2) the percentage of the products in these NAICS industries that will be warehoused for more than six months; (3) the percentage of products warehoused for more than six months that would have required generation of a new label in any particular year due to a manufacturer-initiated labeling change; and (4) the percentage of all products in the NAICS industries covered by the HCS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA calculates cost savings for affected industries by multiplying Columns 3, 4, and 5 in its tables (see Table VI-17 and VI-18). Example: summing industry cost savings yielded an estimated annual cost savings of $33.3 million. Sensitivity tests adjust individual factors (e.g., percent warehoused requiring relabeling) to show proportional impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labeling requirements for small containers (<=100 ml)
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph (f)(12)(ii) allows manufacturers, importers, and distributors to use an abbreviated label on containers with a volume capacity of 100 ml or less when they can demonstrate it is not feasible to use pull-out/fold-back labels or tags to provide full label information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abbreviated label must include product identifier, pictogram(s), signal word, manufacturer's name and phone number, and a statement that full label information is provided on the immediate outer package. OSHA assumed no incremental cost savings from this provision in the PEA because prior letters of interpretation already provided practical accommodations; stakeholders were invited to comment on that determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labeling requirements for very small containers (<=3 ml)
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph (f)(12)(iii) permits only the product identifier on containers with volume capacity of 3 ml or less if the manufacturer, importer, or distributor can demonstrate that any label would interfere with the normal use of the container.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA estimated affected labels and unit cost savings ($0.051 in PEA, updated to $0.058 in 2022 dollars), and multiplied by number of affected labels to derive annual cost savings (estimated $1.7 million). The provision applies only where feasibility demonstrations support inability to use any label or an abbreviated label.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstration requirement for small/very small container exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: To use abbreviated labels (<=100 ml) or product-identifier-only labels (<=3 ml), manufacturers/importers/distributors must demonstrate infeasibility of using pull-out/fold-back labels or tags, and for very small containers that any label would interfere with normal use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA limited cost savings estimates to containers for which such demonstrations could be expected to succeed (e.g., estimated 40 percent of potential very small-container labels). Comments were solicited on feasibility and magnitude of savings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitivity analysis methodology for FEA
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct isolated changes to individual cost input parameters to determine effects on estimated annualized net cost savings; assume methodology/calculations are generally linear and additive so sensitivity is generally proportional to isolated variations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided: changing percent warehoused requiring relabeling from 1% to 0.5% reduces savings by ~50%; doubling to 2% increases savings by ~100%. Other tests include changing percent of very small containers affected, applying familiarization costs to all firms, doubling labor hours for SDS/label revisions, excluding overhead from loaded wages, and lowering discount rate from 7% to 3% (each test reports resulting dollar and percent changes). OSHA uses sensitivity tests for informational robustness checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic feasibility screening test — pass-through (price elasticity = 0)
rubrics_metrics.description: If all costs are passed through to customers (price elasticity of demand = 0), OSHA generally considers a standard economically feasible for an industry when the annualized costs of compliance are less than one percent of annual revenues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasoning: impacts under this threshold are unlikely to eliminate an industry or significantly alter its competitive structure; common price variations typically exceed 3% per year. OSHA notes unusual circumstances may require further analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic feasibility screening test — absorbed costs (infinite elasticity)
rubrics_metrics.description: If all costs are absorbed by firms (infinite price elasticity), OSHA generally considers a standard economically feasible for an industry when the annualized costs of compliance are less than ten percent of annual profits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: Normal year-to-year profit variations can exceed 40%, so a 10% threshold is a modest check against imperiling an industry. OSHA compares compliance costs to profits as a second check.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry-level screening via cost-to-revenue and cost-to-profit ratios
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare estimated annualized compliance costs for each affected industry sector (at six-digit NAICS level) with industry revenues and profits, presenting impacts as ratios of compliance costs to revenues and to profits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA constructs Tables (e.g., VI-21, VI-22) showing revenues, profits, and corresponding estimated annualized costs; for firms obtaining no monetized cost savings, use gross positive costs as numerator. Use these ratios to assess economic feasibility and small-entity impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory alternatives analysis requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe and analyze regulatory alternatives relative to the final rule, presenting midpoint estimates for costs/benefits and quantifying impacts of removing specific provisions (e.g., removing changes to paragraph (f)(12) or (f)(11)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA compared two alternatives: (1) eliminate changes for very small containers (reduces cost savings by $1.7M); (2) eliminate released-for-shipment changes (reduces savings by $33.3M and could yield net costs). Conclude whether alternatives alter feasibility or small-entity impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final Regulatory Flexibility Analysis (FRFA) required elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The FRFA must contain: (1) a statement of the need for, and objectives of, the rule; (2) a statement of significant issues raised by public comments and any changes made in response; (3) the agency response to comments by the Chief Counsel for Advocacy of the SBA and any resulting changes; (4) a description/estimate of the number of small entities to which the rule will apply or why not available; (5) a description of projected reporting, recordkeeping and other compliance requirements (including classes of small entities affected and needed professional skills); and (6) a description of steps taken to minimize significant economic impacts on small entities consistent with statutory objectives, including factual/policy/legal reasons for selected alternatives and why others were rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA may perform FRFA elements in conjunction with other analyses if they satisfy the statutory requirements (5 U.S.C. 605(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Final Regulatory Flexibility Screening Assessment (FRFSA) procedure and certification
rubrics_metrics.description: If the agency determines the final rule will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities, a FRFA is not required; OSHA nonetheless may prepare a voluntary FRFSA summarizing analysis relevant to small entities and certifying no significant impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA prepared a voluntary FRFSA to summarize key aspects of the FEA affecting small businesses and to explain why a full FRFA is not required. The FRFSA includes tables comparing costs and cost savings for small and very small entities and applies screening criteria (one percent of revenues or five percent of profits for small entities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Screening criteria for significant economic impact on small entities
rubrics_metrics.description: For determining significant economic impact on small firms, OSHA assesses whether, for small entities in any given industry, annualized costs exceed one percent of revenues or five percent of profits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA applied these thresholds to Tables VI-23 through VI-26 for small and very small entities; finding no industries exceeded thresholds, OSHA certified no significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions and counts for affected small and very small entities
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate the number of small entities (as defined by SBA) and very small entities (fewer than 20 employees) affected by the rule, and use these counts in the FRFSA/FEA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA estimated 114,585 establishments (within 106,017 firms) as small, and 84,754 very small establishments (within 83,952 firms) as very small, and used these populations in impact tables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Projected reporting, recordkeeping, compliance requirements and unit time burdens
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe compliance requirements (updated classification criteria, simplified labeling for small containers, strengthened SDS awareness, modernized definitions) and estimate unit time burdens and associated hourly wage rates for tasks like SDS revisions, appendix language revisions, management familiarization, and training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example unit burdens and wages provided: Health & Safety Specialist fully loaded hourly wage $61.18 — SDS reclassification: medium establishments 1.5 hours/SDS, small 2.1 hours/SDS; revisions to appendix language: medium 0.5 hrs/SDS, small 0.7 hrs/SDS; management familiarization: medium directly affected 4.0 hrs/establishment, medium indirectly 1.0 hr, small directly 1.0 hr, small indirectly 0.25 hr. Training per affected firm: 2.5 hrs Health & Safety Specialist ($61.18/hr), 0.2 hrs Logistics Personnel ($60.37/hr), 0.2 hrs Production Worker ($31.09/hr).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification responsibilities for manufacturers/importers and employers
rubrics_metrics.description: Chemical manufacturers and importers must evaluate chemicals produced or imported to classify hazard classes and categories; employers are not required to perform classification if they choose to rely on the manufacturer's/importer's classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For each chemical, the manufacturer/importer must determine applicable hazard classes and categories. OSHA notes the compliance costs for those businesses not already aligned with revisions (unit time burdens summarized).

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentration-range approach and CBI trade-secret balancing
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph (i) prescribes reasonably narrow concentration ranges that may be used in combination to preserve trade secrets while disclosing sufficient information on chemical properties to communicate workplace hazards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA believes the final ranges strike a balance between preventing significant economic impacts and disclosure of chemical information. Claiming trade secrets (and thus using the ranges) is optional; firms concerned about costs can choose not to claim and thereby avoid costs associated with the provision. OSHA considered stakeholder comments alleging market/competitive impacts but found no evidence demonstrating likely loss of CBI under the final ranges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of overhead and wage-loading consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensitivity test excluding overhead costs from fully loaded hourly wages to align with 2012 FEA treatment: remove 17% overhead factor from base wages used in cost analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applying this change increased estimated net cost savings by about $0.5 million annually (~2%), demonstrating the quantitative effect of including/excluding overhead in loaded wage calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of discount rate for annualizing costs
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA uses a seven-percent discount rate as the reference point for annualizing costs but examines effects of lowering to three percent in sensitivity analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lowering discount rate from 7% to 3% increased annualized net cost savings from $29.8M to $30.7M (about $908,000 more), indicating discount-rate sensitivity is modest in this analysis.
